title: Checkpoint: Hip-Hop, Electronic and Beyond
objective: After this level you can explain how turntables, synthesizers and computers changed music.
summary: Roland's TR-808 (1980) synthesized drums from circuits; dismissed and discontinued, it powered Planet Rock (1982). Turntables, synths and computers remade music, often by accident.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: the drum machine the critics dismissed.
cards.body: Roland's TR-808 came out in 1980. Critics complained it didn't sound like real drums, and Roland stopped making it after selling about 12,000. Then hip-hop producers got hold of it. Its story ties together this whole chapter's machines.

cards.headline: Drums built from circuits
cards.body: The 808 didn't play recordings of drums. Roland's engineers used analog synthesis, manipulating electrical currents like Level 84's synthesizers, to make sounds that imitated hand-claps and bass notes. That's why critics called it fake, and why its thundering bass became famous. In 1982, Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force's "Planet Rock," made with an 808, became one of the decade's most influential records.

events.label: Kool Herc loops breaks on two turntables in the Bronx
"Planet Rock" puts the 808 at hip-hop's heart

cards.headline: The chapter in one breath
cards.body: Turntables became instruments at Bronx parties. Synthesizers turned electric waves into notes, and the 808 turned circuits into drums. Computers turned songs into numbers small enough to stream. Again and again, the new sound came from using a machine in a way nobody planned: two copies of one record, a pitch fixer pushed into a robot voice, a flop drum machine turned legend.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: How hip-hop grew from Bronx block parties, where DJs turned turntables into instruments.
